newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage-backeds off in slow Monday trading.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage-backeds off in slow Monday trading.

text.p: U.S. mortgage-backed securities languished in very thin trading on Monday, traders said.
One of the few issues sighted was a "large" chunk of adjustable-rate mortgage pools linked to a cost of funds (COFI) index, one trader said.
"There's a large West Coast seller ... and a lot of people think its gotten cheap enough to buy," the trader said.
While most ARMs are tied to CMT (constant maturity Treasury) indices, COFI-linked mortgages offer borrowers and investors more stability, said David Berson, a Fannie Mae economist.
COFI generally refers to the Eleventh Federal Home Loan Bank Bank District's cost of funds, Berson said.
"It is a less-volatile index than, say, a Treasury index," he said, adding that COFI is attractive when market interest rates are heading up but not when they are in decline.
Pass-throughs turned in a mixed performance, heading 5/32 to 13/32 below Friday's closing prices by late Monday afternoon.
Ginnie Mae 30-year 7.5-percent coupons were off 11/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 111 basis points over comparable Treasuries.
Fannie Mae 30-year 7.5-percent had slid 10/32 to 99-16/32, and comparable Freddie Macs were off 10/32 at 99-23/32.
Late in the day, the 10-year Treasury note yield stood at 6.52 percent.
